categories.label: Sources of Contractual Ambiguity Addressed by NLP
categories.memo: Covers the linguistic and drafting problems—vagueness, incompleteness, contradiction, bias—that NLP research targets in construction contracts.

codes.label: Vague/ambiguous obligation language
codes.description: Lack of clarity about roles and obligations is a leading cause of disputes, motivating NLP-based clarification tools.

codes.label: Biased or 'poisonous' risk-shifting clauses
codes.description: Owners sometimes insert clauses that disproportionately shift risk to contractors; NLP can help detect such bias.

codes.label: Incomplete or missing requirements
codes.description: Incomplete project requirements, especially in subcontracts, generate disagreements; automated extraction can flag gaps.

codes.label: Contradictory clauses within a contract
codes.description: Contracts often contain internally inconsistent clauses that current NLP research has not yet adequately addressed.

codes.label: Requirement change-impact tracing
codes.description: Need for tools that trace how modifying one requirement affects others, to preserve consistency across the contract.

codes.label: Modification-induced inconsistency in standard forms
codes.description: Client modifications to standard forms (FIDIC, NEC) introduce inconsistencies that are a leading cause of disputes.

categories.label: NLP/Text-Mining Applications for Obligation and Claim Analysis
categories.memo: Concrete NLP techniques applied to extract obligations, classify claim documents, and support contract administration.

codes.label: Obligation extraction via NLP classification
codes.description: Classification models separate DB contract requirements (design/construction/O&M) to extract subcontractor scope automatically.

codes.label: Owner obligation analysis gap
codes.description: Existing NLP work focuses on contractor obligations; owner obligations (payment, site access, approvals) remain under-studied and vary across standard forms.

codes.label: Lexicon-based obligation extraction
codes.description: Rule-based text-mining approaches (promisor noun + obligation verb patterns) systematically extract and quantify contractual obligations and their risk levels.

codes.label: Claim document classification
codes.description: Automated classification of correspondence and claim documents (contract, project activity, contemporary records) reduces manual, error-prone review.

sub_codes.label: Recall vs. precision trade-off
sub_codes.description: Classifier selection must balance capturing all relevant claim documents (recall) against avoiding false positives (precision/accuracy).(Study 12)

codes.label: Machine learning coding of particular conditions
codes.description: ML-based coding of contract text (Control/Coordination/Adaptation functions) improves objectivity and efficiency in analyzing risk-related clauses.

codes.label: Litigation/claim outcome prediction
codes.description: Predictive models using historical case data could help parties assess claim merit before litigation, an underexplored area.

codes.label: FIDIC particular-conditions classification
codes.description: Text-analytic classification of particular conditions clauses to study how project-specific modifications alter general conditions' functions.

categories.label: Contract Readability and Drafting Quality
categories.memo: Focuses on linguistic and stylistic factors affecting how comprehensible contracts are to practitioners, and how this feeds into dispute risk.

codes.label: Standard form readability comparisons
codes.description: FIDIC and NEC are generally more readable than bespoke contracts, but readability varies by drafting philosophy and jargon use.

codes.label: Legal jargon and technical language barriers
codes.description: Legal language is not native to engineers, making contract reading difficult; excessive jargon in forms like FIDIC reduces clarity.

codes.label: Sentence-length and grammar trade-offs
codes.description: Shortening sentences to improve readability can inadvertently increase grammatical errors (e.g., missing nouns), undermining clarity goals.

codes.label: Root-cause analysis of readability risks
codes.description: Interventions targeting one readability risk can worsen another (butterfly-effect), requiring holistic root-cause analysis rather than simple risk ranking.

codes.label: Visual/diagrammatic contract representation
codes.description: Diagrams and visual representations can increase transparency and reduce reliance on lengthy ambiguous text.

categories.label: Digital Model–Contract Text Interoperability
categories.memo: Addresses how contract text interacts with digital models (BIM) and standard forms, particularly regarding authoritative documents and liability.

codes.label: 2D drawings as legally binding despite 3D/BIM use
codes.description: Contracts often retain 2D drawings as the authoritative legal document even when 3D BIM models drive design and fabrication.

codes.label: Regulatory reliance on 2D stamped drawings
codes.description: Permitting authorities' requirement for 2D stamped drawings constrains contractual reliance on digital models for fabrication-ready workflows.

codes.label: Model authorship, ownership and licensing
codes.description: Clear contractual definition of model element authorship and licensing is needed so downstream fabricators can legally rely on model data.

codes.label: Lack of standard BIM contract forms
codes.description: Absence of standardized BIM contract forms is a major external barrier to BIM/digital adoption, with direct effects on project performance.

codes.label: Owner-mandated software vs. contractor fabrication capability
codes.description: Owner requirements for specific BIM authoring tools can conflict with contractors' existing CNC/prefabrication equipment, forcing contract language adjustments.

categories.label: AI/Automated Contract Analysis for Modular and Off-Site Construction
categories.memo: Applies contract-text analysis concerns specifically to modular/off-site/industrialized construction, where standard forms and specifications are often mismatched.

codes.label: Mismatch of standard forms with modular/off-site delivery
codes.description: Standard forms are frequently modified for modular projects, and literature highlights unique procurement/specification mismatches for precasters and modular contractors.

codes.label: Absence of tailored specifications and codes
codes.description: Lack of separate specifications and building codes for modular/off-site construction contributes to contractual ambiguity requiring text-based classification research.

codes.label: Gap between literature emphasis and litigated case data
codes.description: Despite literature stress on modular/off-site external factors, no analyzed court cases involved such projects, indicating an analytic gap for future contract-text studies.

categories.label: Automated/Self-Executing Contract Mechanisms (Adjacent to Text Analysis)
categories.memo: Captures smart contract and compliance-checking research that overlaps with contract text/administration analysis, distinguished from Theme 4's execution focus by emphasis on governance and documentation gaps.

codes.label: Governance gaps in smart contract stipulations
codes.description: Smart contracts lack mature governance models for rights, obligations and sanctions, limiting flexibility to handle unexpected situations.

codes.label: Automated compliance checking limitations
codes.description: Automated compliance-checking research has focused on late-stage BIM verification, leaving early-stage code-provision selection and quality compliance checking underexplored.

codes.label: Immutable record-keeping trade-offs
codes.description: Blockchain immutability prevents manipulation of progress/delay data but also prevents error correction, raising governance design challenges for fairness.
